entry.title: A lemma from Ross
entry.content:
Just for my own memory, here is a (very intuitive) lemma I struggled to prove in Ross in Huangshan where I stayed up super late with Xqy (to whom I’m grateful) discussing and eventually proving it.

Statement as follows:

\[ orall g,k\in\mathbb{Z}\ with\ gcd(g,k)=1,\ it\ holds\ orall t\in\mathbb{Z}\ \exists a\in\mathbb{Z}\ such\ that\ gcd(t,g+ak)=1.\]

Proof:

Fix such \(g,k\in\mathbb{Z}\) and arbitrary \(t\in\mathbb{Z}\). Factorize \(t=\prod_{i=1}^np_i^{e_i}\).

Consider \(p_i^{e_i}\) for any \(1\leq i\leq n\):

If \(p_i\mid k\) and \(p_i mid g\), then \(gcd(p_i^{e_i},g+ak)=1\) for any \(a\in\mathbb{Z}\).

If \(p_i mid k\), then \(gcd(p_i^{e_i},k)=1\). Proceed as follows:

Let set \(T=\{a\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{0\}: a<p_i^{e_i}\}\) and \(S=\{g+ak:a\in T\}\).

Let function \(f:S ightarrow T\) by \(g+ak\mapsto g+ak\mod{p_i^{e_i}}\).

If \(g+a_1k \equiv g+a_2k\mod{p_i^{e_i}}\) (and we know \(gcd(p_i^{e_i},k)=1\)), then \(p_i^{e_i}\mid (a_2-a_1)\).

This then implies \(a_2=a_1\) by definition of \(T\), so \(f\) is injective.

By injectivity, we have \(T = f(S)\), which then implies \(\exists a_i\in T\) such that \(g+a_ik\equiv 1\mod{p_i^{e_i}}\) and so \(gcd(g+a_ik, p_i^{e_i})=1\).

Finally, by Chinese Reminder Theorem (which I completely forget now), we get \(\exists a\in\mathbb{Z}\) such that \(a\equiv a_i \mod{p_i^{e_i}}\) for all \(i\) where \(p_i mid k\). And for this \(a\), one can check \(gcd(g+ak,t)=1\).

entry.title: How statistical research is telling the false

link.title: How statistical research is telling the false

entry.content:
Let us consider a (highly simplified) research subject where a publication consists of (1) a hypothesis $H_0$ for testing, and (2) a numerical experiment indicating that it’s $p$-value is less than $0.05$. We say this publication rejects $H_0$. For now, suppose only statistically significant works get published.

Claim as follows: \(For\ each\ hypothesis\ H_0\ that\ holds\ true,\exists\ a\ publication\ that\ rejects\ H_0\ after\ \widetilde{O}(1)\\\ failed\ publication\ attempts\ with\ high\ probability.\)

A failed publication attempt refers to a time when an experiment for testing $H_0$ (which holds true) is conducted but $p$-value is above $0.05$. This result is rather straightforward; since $H_0$ holds, the probablity of getting statistical significance is $0.05$. Standard concentration results indicate that, with probability at least $1-\delta$, there is a statistically significant trial in $O(\log(1/\delta))$ experiments. There is an implicit assumption that the repeated experiments testing $H_0$ are independent, i.e. the later efforts run their own trials and their outcomes are independent from the existing (unpublished) ones.

Note that this claim remains true even if statistically insignificant works are published, as long as experiment independence among the publications remains to hold. This model is for sure highly hand-weavy and overly simplified, but a few implications (as well as those unrealistic simplifications) are highlighted:

Simplifications:

  • A publication surely consists more than just a hypothesis testing. There is also data analysis and causality study, which are more fundamental.
  • The experiments are heterogeneous, and “$H_0$ holds true under the experiments” is not properly defined.
  • …

Implications:

  • One shouldn’t take statistical significance as hypothesis rejection.
  • Statistically insignificance works should be weighted equally. For now I believe the majority of them are either unpublished or published but largely overlooked.
  • For each hypothesis, since it is proposed, the time it gets “rejected” depends on the “frequency” that it gets tested by independent experiments. This frequency in turn depends on the population size of the research community and its popularity. So the larger the community is and the more popular the hypothesis is, the sooner it sees a rejecting publication.
  • From the audience’s perspective, when facing a collection of such publications, there is no reliable way of telling which hypotheses are false, and which hypotheses are falsely rejected (as long as this research subject, or the hypotheses of interest, stands over a history long enough to include $\widetilde{O}(1)$ repeated experiments).

entry.title: Should I clear my plate?
entry.content:
Clearing the plate has been an advocated act in my upbringing and an act that I faithfully sticked to. I had believed in that one should always clear the plate for various ethical reasons, e.g. not wasting social resources especially when many people around the world still starve, or simply saving some money for my family by wasting less.

Then my faithful strategy was penalized by the adversary in the dining table: when I was in the primary school, my mom, who believed I was overly lean and knew my clearing-plate strategy, deliberately cooked much more than the family could normally take every time. Then I quickly became over 2x heavier because I had to ate up everything.

Until then I realized my strategy was so vulnerable in terms of my own utility. While I tried to act otherwise, I also tried to un-justify it, i.e. maybe clearing our plates is not that morally laudable. Indeed, conditioned on an excessive amount of food is served, taking a comfortable amount maximizes our (or just my) utility, because gaining more weight than wanted has a long-term effect and potentially large cost on emotion and time (to lose weight). If you’re in a restaurant, they deal with waste anyway, so you add little marginal cost on them and on the society if the waste is dealt with properly.

It is however not saying we give up on saving food. I now believe the best practice is to ask everyone follow a good ordering (or cooking if at home) strategy:

  • Estimate roughly how much you (or the whole party) can comfortably consume;
  • Order (cook) 80~90% of your estimate;
  • Have a running estimate of how much you’ve ordered based on the served dishes;
  • Order more if you underestimated.

Then you save everything including your money, the edible resources of the society, the resources for decomposing waste, etc. It’s also always better to eat less than eat more, as you can obviously have snacks / desserts afterwards.

entry.title: Inequality for norms of matrix producted with projection

link.title: Inequality for norms of matrix producted with projection

entry.content:
Suppose we have an arbitrary \(m​\)-by-\(n​\) matrix \(M​\) and any subspaces \(A\subseteq B​\) in \(n​\)-dim. Let \(P_{A,B}​\) denote the projection matrix to \(A,B​\) respectively. We want to compare the norms of \(MP_A​\) and \(MP_B​\) that are related to the singular values.

First and most obvious, the operator norm (induced by some arbitrary vector norm):

\[\begin{align*} \|MP_A\|_{op} \equiv \sup_{x\in A,\|x\|=1}\|Mx\| \leq \|MP_B\|_{op}. \end{align*}\]

Second, the Frobenius norm, observe \(MP_A=MP_BP_A\):

\[\begin{align*} \|MP_A\|_F^2 &= \|(MP_BP_A)^T\|_F^2\\ &= \|P_A^TP_B^TM^T\|_F^2\\ &\leq \|P_A^T\|_{op}\|P_B^TM^T\|_F^2\\ &=\|MP_B\|_F^2\quad\quad\quad\text{when $\|P_A^T\|_{op}=\|P_A\|_{op}=1$, i.e. $A$ is not null space} \end{align*}\]

Third, the nuclear norm follows immediately from the above observation:

\[\begin{align*} \|MP_A\|_* = \|MP_BP_A\|_* \leq \|MP_B\|_* \end{align*}\]

since \(\|QV\|_*=\sum_i\sigma_i(QV)\leq \sum_i\sigma_i(Q)\|V\|_{op} = \|Q\|_*\|P\|_{op}\) where operator norm gives the largest singular value.
